The annual session of the Peacebuilding Commission is called to order. Secretary-General, ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this annual session of the Peacebuilding Commission, whose theme is UN Peacebuilding Architecture, celebrating 20 years of the UN Peacebuilding Architecture. This session offers us an opportunity to do the following: 1, learn the lessons from the journey so far; 2, welcome progress made; and 3, contemplate the means that the PBC may use to continue to strengthen partnerships for innovation, inclusion, and impact. I wish to thank each and every one of you for your presence, and I wish to say how deeply grateful I am to the distinguished speakers that do us the honor taking the floor today, namely Mr.— His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations Organization; Her Excellency Madame Leonor Zalabata Torres, President of the Security Council and Ambassador Permanent Representative of Colombia to the United Nations; His Excellency Mr. Bernardo Arévalo, President of the Republic of Guatemala; Her Excellency Ms. Sara Bayesloyo Nyante, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Liberia, and Her Excellency Miss Sandra Polemon, Minister of Planning and External Cooperation of Haiti. I now move to the first item on our agenda, that is my introductory remarks. Secretary-General, President of the Security Council, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great privilege to open this annual session in the very same room where 20 years ago the United Nations put their weight behind a belief that came to define an age. That belief that peace, once won, had to be preserved, and that it could only be preserved If we acted in unity, no man could do it alone. This anniversary invites us to honor a cause as much as a date, the cause that gave birth to the PBC. Those who gave rise to the PBC bequeathed us a conviction that is a conviction that the years have only served to confirm. Incidentally, no peace is irreversible, and any and all peace remains something that we have to preserve collectively and together and can only last if we do that. 20 years later, this lesson is no longer called into question. That is the idea that peace cannot be imposed by a diktat from outside. It is built from within. It is the, it is the fruit of a partnership and cannot be bestowed by a mandate. Peace does not last because it was financed for years. It lasts because it is appropriate, maintained, and renewed by each and every individual who brought it about. For two decades, our consolidation has fully discharged the mandate of its founding resolution, and we continue to support this mandate over the course of time. There are international financial institutions, development regional organizations, civil society, and the private sector. They, too, must work to preserve peace. They've worked with the PBC. Through the PBF, the PBC has mobilized more than $1.9 billion and— for the benefit of more than 60 countries, thanks to the generosity of more than 70 contributing states. The PBF and PBC above all enshrined a sacred principle: No peace can can take root without the ownership of the people affected. This 20th anniversary paves the way for the work forward, and we remember the first PBC week that we held. Every item, every word in the topic for today's meeting was carefully chosen. Inclusion is vital because a peace that excludes women, its young people, and its communities is but a truth, a temporary truth and never a permanent aki. Impact is crucial because our people will judge us not on our intentions but on what has changed in their daily lives. Innovation, too, is crucial. Through the adoption by consensus of the PBA resolutions and the recent resolution on the review of our peacebuilding architecture, member states charted a new course for national ownership. That was its Loadstar. Prevention was the primary goal. They invited for international financial institutions and regional banks, regional development banks, to stand alongside us and called for more deeply rooted, broader partnerships and better equipped partnerships because a strategy with no resources is but an empty wish. An ambition stripped of financing is but a promise postponed. We will be guided by the UN Secretary-General. His leadership, his engagement are both tireless, as is his inspiration, and all those qualities have colored our ambition. The President of the Security Council has recalled putting an end to conflicts and building peace is part of one and the same responsibility. And representatives from Guatemala, Liberia, Haiti —will say the same. Their memories have the living—their nations have the living memories of what it means to build peace. We will heed their advice because without partnerships our ambitions are but dead letter. Civil society, development, the private sector—all these are crucial, as are young peacebuilders. They are the masters of their own fate, crafting their present. Today is the 20th anniversary, but we're not marking this event to guarantee the longevity of an institution, but to reaffirm that our cause is a rightful one. We're celebrating this architecture because this architecture has been able to prevail, adapt, and that is because member states have continued to entrust it with an ever more demanding mandate. Over the last 20 years, we've learned to build peace. In the next 20 years, we will be called upon to see peace grow because no generation is handed a complete peace. Everyone is given the opportunity to make a peace more just, broader, more lively, and more lasting than the peace they were first given. Ours is the— we are the ones who have to seize this opportunity today. Let us seize it and make 2030 2030, not the deadline, but the time we really uphold promises made in the past. Thank you. I now have the huge honor of inviting His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations Organization, to issue his address. Excellency, you have the floor.

Saeed Rais. Excellencies, we gather to mark both the 20th anniversary of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture and the first-ever Peacebuilding Week. For two decades, The Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund have helped communities emerge from the darkness of war. That spirit of healing and of hope could not be more vital today. Across the globe, we are witnessing more conflicts than at any point since the Second World War. Geopolitical tensions are rising. Inequalities are deepening. Climate shocks are intensifying. And new technologies are racing ahead without guardrails. All this makes the patient and steady work of peacebuilding more critical than ever. Your task is to imagine a new generation of peace efforts fit to meet the realities of today. Excellencies, the Commission's work over the past 20 years points the way forward. In Colombia, You helped ground peacebuilding in local realities and engaged more women and youth. In the Sahel, you convened across borders to advance the UN Integrated Strategy. In the Central African Republic, you supported the first local elections in 30 years and continue to work with MINUSCA to protect peacekeeping gains that have been obtained. And in Liberia, You helped bridge the gap from the departure of the UN peacekeeping mission to a nationally-owned strategy, rallying stakeholders behind a comprehensive peacebuilding plan. And I could go on and on and on. Through it all, the Commission has never been alone. The Peacebuilding Fund has acted as a catalytic financing instrument, engaging early and taking risks to invest in peace. The Fund has helped more than 70 countries across the globe, backing people and institutions to forge sustainable peace. One of the strengths of this Commission, alongside the Fund and the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office, is its ability to bring together actors across politics, finance and development. And such coordination is what turns commitments into real change on the ground. For countless people, this means services restored, livelihoods rebuilt, justice strengthened and trust renewed. In line with the Pact for the Future, the Commission is also helping countries develop their own national prevention and peacebuilding strategies, from Mauritania to São Tomé e Príncipe. I encourage more States to make use of this platform. It is a place to share progress, seek support and align international partners behind national priorities. Excellencies, last year Member States unanimously adopted the Peacebuilding Architecture Review resolutions. These measures provide a roadmap to build on the work of the Commission. They called for more engagement with outside partners—from civil society to regional organizations, deeper synergies with ECOSOC and the General Assembly, an enhanced advisory role to the Security Council, stronger partnership with international financial institutions and the private sector, and greater assistance for mission transitions as the UN footprint changes and peace operations draw down. Thanks to your support, the introduction of assessed contributions has placed the Peacebuilding Fund on steadier firm footing and a true vote of confidence in its mission. But it still relies on voluntary contributions to invest at the speed and scale peacebuilding demands. I urge all Member States to continue to stand behind it. With your backing, our peacebuilding architecture can advance prevention and recovery efforts around the world. And help keep many more people safe. Monsieur le Président, cher—

Mr. President, dear friends, this Commission was created to nurture the seeds of peace a long time ago so they were able to take root. In an era marked by the proliferation of crises, your mission remains clear: protecting peoples from the scourge of war and helping them rise from the ashes to build better lives. On this anniversary, I urge all Member States to renew their commitment to a future free from violence and to the tools that make such a world possible: international law, sustainable development, and human rights. Together, we can build a peace that lasts everywhere and for all. I thank you.

The Council also recognizes that the full, effective, safe, and meaningful participation of young people is critical in maintaining and promoting international peace and security and advancing peacebuilding and sustaining peace efforts. As the Peacebuilding Commission marks 20 years since Since its establishment, the Security Council wishes to reaffirm its commitment to continued cooperation with the Commission in support of peacebuilding and sustaining peace. Thank you very much.

The commission— the Security Council was established to maintain peace, and the PBC has been undertaking to make these gains a reality over the long term. And the convergence of these efforts will shape a lasting peace. We will now listen to a video message from His Excellency César Bernardo Arévalo de León, President of the Republic of Guatemala.

Since 2011, the Peace Building Fund of the United Nations has supported Guatemala in the implementation of the peace accords that brought an end to the eternal internal armed conflict in 1996. It has invested in supporting our country through more than 25 projects aimed at strengthening the rule of law, justice, and peaceful coexistence. Thanks to this support, legal processes for prosecuting cases related to internal armed conflict have been strengthened and historic progress has been achieved, such as the Sepur Sarko case, a case which provided reparations to women survivors of sexual violence. Marking a milestone in transitional justice and reparations for these victims. Hundreds of victims of the internal armed conflict have been identified and reintegrated into their families with psychosocial support, and more than 60 civil society organizations, including women and youth organizations, have received capacity building to enhance their informed participation in peace-related decision-making processes. The Fund has also strengthened coordination among institutions to prevent electoral conflicts and to improve the protection and reintegration of migrants in Central America through projects such as Peace Infrastructures, InfraPas, More than 600 public officials have been trained, and more than 1,000 members of civil society have participated in dialogue and decision-making processes for conflict transformation. Today, the Peacebuilding Fund directly supports prevention and management of agrarian and territorial conflicts, including including through the work of the Presidential Commission on Conflicts, COPRICON, that also monitors hundreds of cases in territories such as the Polochic Valley. The Fund also supports direct dialogue between the government of the Republic and indigenous peoples. That is a priority of my administration, which has placed the effective participation of indigenous authorities at the very heart of the country's democratic recovery process. Justice, dialogue, and indigenous participation—these have been the pillars of our government for the peace process, a peace process that Guatemala continues to build with the support of the Peace Building Fund. Peace is not a closed chapter of our history. It is an ongoing endeavor of Our democracy, it requires our efforts on a daily basis. Thank you.

Remarks by His Excellency Joseph Nyoman Boikaa, President of the Republic of Liberia. Mr. Secretary-General, Chair of the PBC, ASG Speher, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, distinguished Heads of Agencies, Funds and Programs, peacebuilding partners, members of the diplomatic Community, ladies and gentlemen. Let me begin by conveying my deep appreciation to the Secretary-General and to the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office for the invitation to join this distinguished gathering. It is a great honor for me as President of the Republic of Liberia to be invited to have my country stand among the nations marking 20 years of the Peacebuilding Fund. And I am pleased that you have permitted my Foreign Minister, Madam Sarah Beslon Nyanti, to bring these words to you on my behalf. I regret that the demands of governing our nation at this moment did not allow me to be with you, but I want this assembly to know that Liberia's presence at this anniversary is not a formality. It is personal. It is rooted in our own history and in the long road our people have walked from war to peace. Liberia's story is well known to this organization. For more than a decade, our country was consumed by conflict. Hundreds of thousands of our people were killed. Hundreds of thousands more were displaced. Our institutions were hollowed out, our economy was shattered, and an entire generation of Liberian children grew up knowing the sound of gunfire before they knew the inside of a classroom. I do not recount this history to dwell on pain. I recount it because it is the foundation of everything I will say to you today. Liberia does not speak about peacebuilding as a theory. We speak about it as something we have lived, something we continue to build year by year, often imperfectly, but always with determination. When the guns fell silent in 2003, the world did not turn away from us. The United Nations Mission in Liberia stood beside our people through a long and difficult transition. And when the Peace Building Fund was established, Liberia became one of its earliest partners. Over these 20 years, that partnership has helped us invest in reconciliation, in rule of law, in security sector reform, and in giving young people their stake in their own country's future. The results have been tangible and they have been lasting. The Fund supported rule of law education that brought human rights and legal awareness to communities long before and long beyond the reach of some of the formal institutions that were falling apart. It strengthened our security sector. It built the capacity of police and military through dedicated gender task forces. It empowered women as peacebuilders, supported community peace huts as local spaces for dispute resolution, and funded women's situation rooms that monitored and addressed hundreds of cases of conflict, including election-related violence. It helped communities across Nimba, Cape Mount, Sino, Maryland, and so many other counties better understand and exercise their land rights. Addressing one of the deepest root causes of tension in our society. It has invested in our youth, ensuring that young Liberians are engaged in civic life rather than left vulnerable to manipulation and exclusion. Taken together, these investments help Liberia conduct 3 successive, successive peaceful presidential elections, culminating in the 2023 transfer of power that the world recognized as a milestone in our democratic journey. Mr. Secretary-General, allow me to share briefly what Liberia's journey has taught us about peacebuilding, because I believe these lessons speak to every nation represented in this hall. First, peace is not an event. It is not a ceasefire, and it is not the day a peace agreement is signed. Peace is a continuous generational task. Liberia held its first peace agreement in 2003. We're still doing the work of that agreement. It continues and will continue to build on the findings and recommendations of our Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Second, peacebuilding must be nationally owned. International support was and remains indispensable to Liberia. However, no outside actor can build peace inside a country on its behalf. The Peacebuilding Fund understood this from the start. And it did not impose solutions on Liberia. It invested in Liberian institutions, Liberian leadership, and Liberian ownership of our own recovery. That is why its support has endured, and that is why it matters. Third, reconciliation requires honesty about our past. My administration has taken deliberate steps to confront our history directly, including a national apology to the victims of our civil wars, and the reburial with full state honors of two former presidents who were killed while in office. President Samuel Kanyondo was laid to rest in Zwedru, Grand Gedeh County, his home county, while President William R. Tolbert Jr. was reburied in Montserrado. These reburials, held more than three decades after their deaths, were not merely ceremonial. They were an act of national conscience long overdue, intended to bring closure to grieving families and to a nation that had carried the weight of unresolved history on its shoulders. We also continue our efforts through dignified memorialization and our work to establish a war and economic crimes court. These are not easy undertakings. They surface old wounds. But a peace built on silence is a fragile peace, and Liberia has chosen the harder pathway the more honest path. Fourth, peace and development are inseparable. A peace that does not deliver roads, schools, healthcare, and opportunities will not hold. This is the thinking behind our government's National Development Agenda, which places governance, infrastructure, and human capital at the center of our efforts to consolidate peace and lift our people towards shared prosperity. Excellencies, Liberia comes to this anniversary not only as a recipient of the Peace Building Fund's support, but increasingly as a contributor to the global peacebuilding agenda. As we've taken up our first full term on the non— as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the 2026-2027 term, we have brought into this role the lessons of our own recovery. We have said before, and I will say this again today, that while we sit at this table bearing the name of Liberia, it belongs to the wider community of nations that have known conflict and found their way back to peace. We also recognize that peacebuilding today faces new and pressing tests. Youth unemployment and exclusion threaten to undo hard-won gains across our region. Climate-related shocks are eroding our coastlines and displacing our communities. Mistrust in institutions, if left unaddressed, can unravel decades of progress in a single generation. Liberia urges this organization and this Fund to keep pace with these realities, investing not only in the aftermath of conflict, but the prevention of it. Mr. Secretary-General, on behalf of the people and government of Liberia, I extend our sincere gratitude to the Peacebuilding Fund, to its donors, and to the dedicated staff who have walked with us through some of the most difficult chapters of our national life. 20 years is a milestone worth celebrating, but I would ask this Assembly to mark it not simply by looking back, but by recommitting to the work that remains ahead. Liberia stands ready to continue as a partner in that work, sharing what we have learned, supporting other nations on their own journeys, and continuing to build brick by brick the peace that our people sacrificed so much to achieve. I thank you, and I wish this Peacebuilding Week every success.

Monsieur le Président. Mr. Chairman, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I am taking the floor today on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Haiti. Led by the Prime Minister, Alexis Didier Fils-Aimé, with gravity, clear-sightedness, and hope. The gravity of a country confronting a profound crisis. The clear-sightedness of knowing that peace is not something which can be decreed. This is something which needs to be built. And the hope of a people who refuse to renounce themselves to their future. I welcome this this meeting dedicated to Partnerships for Innovation and Inclusion, and I wish to thank on behalf of the Government of Haiti His Excellency Antonio Guterres for his recent visit to Haiti. Mr. Secretary-General, you have seen the faces behind the statistics. You have met with the women, the children, the young people, the families who experience on a day-to-day basis the devastating consequences of violence, and you reminded the world of a critical truth. Haiti must not be forgotten. When we talk about peacebuilding, we frequently discuss strategies, we discuss financing. Today, I wish to take this opportunity to talk about human beings. I'm thinking of a young Haitian girl who dreamed of becoming a nurse. Violence led to the shuttering of her school. Her family was displaced. She was victimized by sexual violence, being used by a weapon of terror. For a long period of time, she believed that her life was over. And yet today, this young girl is moving forward with the support of other survivors, and she is rebuilding her life. I'm also thinking of a 13-year-old boy who was recruited by gangs. 13, an age when this child should have been learning math and dreaming of his future, he instead was bearing a weapon. Thanks to a reintegration, reinsertion program, he left violence behind him and today is learning a profession and dreaming of opening up his own business. These two stories serve as a reminder of a critical truth that women must not be condemned to remaining victims. Children Children must not be born to become criminals. With opportunities, they can become peacebuilders. And this is why our central message is very clear: Security and safety is indispensable, but this alone does not suffice. It needs to be accompanied by justice, youth employment, protections for women, and the incremental restoration of rule of law and the restoration of trust. Between citizens and institutions. Security cannot result— security alone cannot result in the silencing of weapons, but only peace can result in the rekindling of hope. Peace is not just the absence of violence. Peace is also a family whose children receive nourishment and food. Peace is a mother whose dignity is restored. Peace is a father who returns home with the hope of being able to feed his family, who watches his children sleep believing that tomorrow will be better than today. Peace is a young person who finds a job instead of a gang. Peace is a child who attends school and achieves his dreams. And this is why we believe that the response to this crisis needs to be global, humanitarian, and sustainable in nature, needs to be rooted in an integrated approach, bringing together humanitarian action, peacebuilding, and development. When humanitarian assistance saves lives, When peacebuilding rebuilds trust and when development creates new opportunities, that is when we create the conditions for true stability. I wish to reiterate our government's gratitude to the PBC and the PBF. With more than $50 million invested in Haiti, the PBF has built the capabilities of the state has supported DDR/RBC programs, has facilitated the implementation of the Women, Peace and Security Resolution 1325, as well as ushered in the rehabilitation of community-based infrastructure. We wish today to, to continue this partnership on the basis of three priorities: to protect women and girls, to provide alternatives to young people, and to accelerate the stabilization process for communities. I wish to be clear today: Haiti is not asking for alms. Haiti is not asking for compassion. Haiti is not asking for pity. Haiti is asking for peace, because peace is a global public asset, because all peoples deserve peace, because security does not know— knows no borders, and because hope also knows no borders. And I wish to conclude with a with profound conviction. Every protected girl is a victory for peace. Every woman whose dignity is restored is a victory for peace. Every reconciled community is a victory for peace. And each time we transform a tale of fear into a tale of hope, we help all of humanity progress for Haiti, for succeeding generations, for a peace that will not merely be an ideal, a pipe dream, but a real lived reality. Thank you.

Madam Marie-Laure Akin-Ogbaibe, African Development Bank. How specifically does the bank intend to translate this into a reality for the financing to actively support prevention and peacebuilding on the ground?

Yes, thank you very much. Thank you very much, Chair. My congratulations to you and I wish a happy birthday to the peacebuilding architecture. Throughout the world, on behalf of President Taa, the President of the African Development Bank, we are delighted to receive this invitation. I would like to underline that we've seen four major developments in the way we work. The first is that fragility now—issues of peace, security—are not peripheral issues. No longer trivial sideline issues. They're not niche issues but are entirely integrated into our operations. Whether we be talking about identifying strategies, intervening in various countries, or projects and programs that we support in various countries, in all— across all of those fronts, the issue of resilience and of everything that might contribute to peace is dealt with and addressed. We've developed analytical tools and we also ensure that all of this is put into practice in each of our investments. Now, the second development that we've seen was in response to the Secretary General's appeal. He called upon IFIs to be genuine agents properly committed to peace and working for it. And so we've seen things kind of be turned upside down, and now we focus entirely— well, we focus largely on prevention in everything we do. We could be talking about financing corridors or projects which allow for climate change adaptation. Whatever we're doing, we always ask ourselves the question now: has that extended or broadened opportunities for women, young people, Is what we're financing contributing to social cohesion? That's at the heart of what we do. And so the third point is that we no longer settle for saying we're simply intervening and we're not going to bother about thriving, we're just going to survive. No, we try to be active stakeholders that contribute to peace and security, and we try to ensure that our investments are able to to sustainably contribute to peace. And then the last point, it's very difficult, it's very complex to work in fragile countries, countries in a transition. So there does need to be myriad partnerships. There needs to be a slightly more granular analysis of risks. We need to draw in the private sector. You need to work with civil society. And all of that's a little new for us, but we are taking decisive strides in that direction.

I thank Ms. Ms. Ogbad for her presentation and particularly for the four creeds that she's pointed to as coloring the work of the African Development Bank in terms of peacekeeping on the ground. Mr. Chair, Excellencies, dear colleagues, it's a great pleasure to represent the World Bank Group at this very important day. The World Bank Group's refreshed strategy that will cover the period 2026 2030—it was launched earlier this month at the World Bank Group Fragility Forum—places prevention and resilience at the center of our engagement. The core lesson is simple: prevention is most effective when it is nationally led, grounded in local realities, and supported early before risks deepen into full crisis. For the Bank, supporting nationally led prevention and peacebuilding means helping countries address the underlying drivers of fragility. Including exclusion, weak institutions, regional disparities, lack of economic opportunity, and pressures linked to displacement or climate stress. Our role is not political mediation. It is to bring development financing, analytical tools and knowledge, and long-term support for institutions, services, and livelihoods in ways that strengthen resilience and reduce the risk to escalation. We are seeing this approach, for example, in practice in Niger, where prevention and resilience financing from the World Bank Group supported the government's action plan to expand opportunities for youth and women, strengthen state presence in border areas with services, and reduce tensions over natural resources and access to justice. Across this context, one point is especially important: jobs, more and better jobs, matter. Productive economic opportunities, especially for young people, are essential not only for growth and poverty reduction but also for dignity, inclusion, and confidence in the future.

When Madam said happy birthday, I almost thought it was your birthday, but it's the birthday of the Peacebuilding Fund. Excellencies, ACORD has had the privilege of engaging with the peacebuilding support architecture from the beginning. From that experience and from over 3 decades of supporting peace across Africa, I would say that the most effective partnerships have three distinguishing features. First, they are anchored in national and local ownership, not as a slogan but as a discipline. Peacebuilding cannot be imported. External partners can accompany, resource, convene, and protect spaces, but legitimacy must come from the society itself. Secondly, effective partnerships are built on trust must before crisis. Civil society is most useful when it is brought in only after violence has escalated, but when it is already embedded in communities, able to read early warning signs, and trusted enough to speak honestly to governments, communities, and international actors. Thirdly, the best partnerships are politically informed but not politically captured. Civil society can often operate in the sensitive spaces between state and society, between formal institutions and communities, and between national actors and external partners. But this requires respect for its independence and impartiality. And lastly, for ACORD, the lesson is clear, Chair. Nationally led peacebuilding works best when civil society is treated not as an implementing contractor, but as a strategic partner in sustaining dialogue, rebuilding trust and strengthening the social compact.

Thank you. Sure, merci, Monsieur.

I wish to thank Mr. Gundin for those thoughts and I now invite Ms. Linda Dumper, General Director of the Adeba Laboratories, to join the discussion by responding to the following question. The small and medium-sized enterprises play in long-term peacebuilding efforts a decisive multidimensional role which goes far beyond merely creating jobs. As best as they can, they contribute to tackling the structural drivers of conflicts, inequalities, exclusion, weak institutions, all the while they strengthen stability and resilience. Could you tell us some more about your trajectory, about the way in which you integrate the takeaways from your discussion— you've the way in which you integrate the repercussions of your business decisions into your community-level activities.

Thank you. So while at Adeba, the biocosmetic company I founded with my mother, a pharmacist, to provide alternatives to petrocosmetics that are dangerous for our health and our environment, I received 3 phone calls that my MBA from Harvard and my years at McKinsey did not prepare me for. The first two sent a wave of panic. My colleague Armel, who works in the northern part of Côte d'Ivoire, was threatened with bodily harm. In the first situation, he just wanted to pack up and leave. In the second situation, he suffered severe burns from being struck by illegal gold miners fleeing the local police. The third phone call brought tears to my eyes. Armelle had just given her wage to one of the rural women we work with, and she just started crying, revealing to him that she now had the money to go to the market to buy food for her 3 children. So the lessons from those calls highlight the ripple effects that my work has, and why it's so important to consider it. First lesson: we didn't end up leaving. The community rallied around us, and the chief of the village placed us under his protection. So we hired rural women, and they saved us. Second lesson: jobs are a matter of safety. And for us, that means creating the ecosystem that supports dignified jobs. And we're doing so by co-creating the first regional biocosmetic master, a UNESCO chair that unites Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, and Guinea. Third, entrepreneurs of the Harambee Alliance that brought me here today have chosen to make growth inclusive so that the words of our pledge manifest and become true, that the Africa that our generation desires—peaceful, beautiful, powerful—can be won. It exists. It is real. It is possible. And it is ours.

I thank Ms. Dompah for those forceful responses and particularly for the conviction which emanates from everything you say. I now wish to turn towards Mr. Issa Touré Shamsou of UNOI Peacebuilders. Mstoa, young people are often presented as vital partners in peacebuilding. However, many of them often continue to come up against obstacles stymieing effective participation, both in terms of accessing decision-making fora and resources. In light of your personal experience, in specific terms, what does a true partnership with young people peacebuilders look like, and how can such a partnership contribute to producing more powerful results in terms of peacebuilding?

Yes, thank you so much, the Chair and Your Excellencies, for the opportunity to be here. First of all, the very useful partnerships that I have seen are partnerships that are built under co-leadership, co-ownership, and co-investing. In this case, you are co-designing projects with young people and trusting in their abilities and their capacities. That's the first one. The second is that we see partnerships that goes beyond financing are much more sustainable. Partnership here not necessarily providing funds for the activities and projects of young people, but investing in themselves, their capacity, investing in their networks, their groups, then that makes it sustainable partnership. The third and important is that young people, including myself, are getting tired of being consulted all the time on how can we work with you. We want to move from how can we work with you into now how— what are the best practices in working with young people, because the information is already there. We've participated in several consultations, and we have given you already so many ideas on how to work with us, so we are asking that question. Let's move from how do we work with young people to what are the best practices in working with young people. And finally, when we are able to develop initiatives that are co-led by young people, when we finance young people beyond just giving them money for projects, but invest in their protection, invest in creating enabling environment, invest in their capacity building, and also moving from just consultation into sharing best practices,, we would be moving many steps closer to sustainable peace. Thank you.

I thank Mr. Shamsu for those thoughts. I just wish to add that the more we listen to young people, the more we develop the conviction that they need to be given a greater place within any dialogue, discussion, or program focusing on peace building. After that first round of questions, I am now going to I'll pose you questions in the same order. I'll pose a series of additional questions to you in that order. Please be as brief as possible. First, I turn to you, Ms. Akın Uğurbek. From the point of view of implementation, where do you see the most promising possibilities as being located in terms of aligning development financing to prevention goals peace-building goals and how do you see increasing the impact of that financing, namely through closer cooperation with the PBC?

Merci beaucoup. Thank you very much indeed. I'm really delighted to note that there is good— the various panelists seem to think along the same lines. My fellow panelists have said something that I think is very important. It's very important for us to grow more powerful in terms of everything related to investments, but both financed investments and grey investments, across all investments that make it possible to tackle the root causes of fragility. Those investments need to grow in size. We might be talking about job creation or creating ecosystems which make it possible to create jobs. We might be talking about tackling the issue of food insecurity, whatever we're focusing on, it's important to guarantee that we go beyond having these isolated piecemeal projects. My colleague said just that. Instead, we need to work on platforms where we co-invest or co-create alongside primary beneficiaries. That's what we do, for example, in Mozambique. There, we've contributed to the creation of what we call an SME village in a region in the north of Mozambique. There, the primary cause of fragility is the sense of marginalization. Young people feel excluded. They see prosperity, they see major infrastructure projects springing up, but they can't participate. So this village makes it possible to create very close links between procurement processes or the tenders of these sent out by these major construction groups, links between that and these SMEs. We've created a hub called the Peace and Security Investment Hub. There we support a number of young people in creating companies, small and medium-sized enterprises, to allow them to better harness the opportunities that have been created in their region where they live They don't need to travel anywhere, but this work also guarantees that they're a stakeholder and entirely abreast of what's happening in the business ecosystem. We should also continue to build institutions. That's something very specific. We have to have institutions which inspire trust, institutions that are accountable, And first and foremost, institutions which guarantee that no one is marginalized as far as possible. And finally, and I said this, I think, we need to continue to advocate for investment in prevention. There are statistics, I think, that every dollar invested in prevention saves $16, $17, $18, depending on what methodologies you use. Because that money doesn't need to be spent on conflict resolution. We need to do more, and we also need to demonstrate that our efforts pay off and produce tangible, tangible results. And there we see a very important role for our partnership with the Peacebuilding Fund. We need to look at how together we can jointly create, hand in hand with key stakeholders, these solutions that allow us to scale things up very quickly. Everyone can't just remain in their domain of choice. We need to break out of these silos and tailor efforts to domestic national priorities. Many countries have good prevention— conflict prevention systems, and we need to support those systems with the Peacebuilding Fund that has that convening power. That ability to bring people together. And then, of course, there's the political lens and we need to use that because we as financial institutions don't have that. You have political will, you have the means of implementation also.

I do want to thank you for the emphasis you've placed on helping young people in fragile areas where they are marginalized. You touched on the example from the north of Mozambique. As we know, there violent extremism, terrorism, they feed off the marginalization of young people and we commend the work— the African Development Bank for supporting the PBC, particularly In the wake of work done by the PBC previously, particularly in Africa, I now wish to turn towards Ms. Dimitriadou. Ms. Dimitriadou, the Security Council and the General Assembly have called for a close partnership between the UN and IFIs in peacebuilding contexts. What advice, if I might call it advice, would you give to the PBC to make good on that ambition?

Let me build on the excellent points by my colleague by the African Development Bank. If I may offer a practical suggestion, that would be to continue strengthening the bridge between the Peacebuilding Commission's convening role and nationally-led development action. The PBC is not an operating a financing platform, but its convening, its political role is extremely important. It can help sustain attention on national prevention priorities, support coherence across the UN system and international financial institutions, keep peacebuilding perspectives connected to longer-term institutional building and economic recovery. This is extremely important because in fragile settings in particular, partnership we see works best when it's organized around nationally-led frameworks rather than around parallel systems. And we heard that from previous speakers before. Let me give you a good example, Chad, where support from the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund has been complemented by the World Bank investments aiming at strengthening resilience and addressing drivers of fragility. So that would be my one piece of suggestion or advice, if I can call it like that, to use the PBC's convening power to bring political peacebuilding and development actors together early around nationally defined priorities. And this is how partnership becomes coherent, more country-driven, and more effective. Let me close by restating our commitment at the World Bank Group to continue working with the PBC, with the UN system, with development partners, private sector, civil society, society for long-lasting peace and prosperity. Thank you.

I wish to thank Ms. Dimitriadou for that response, and I just want to confirm a truth, and that is cooperation with the PBC, particularly the country-specific configurations, has never been as fertile or intense as in your case. I can bear witness to that because I am the chair of the Central African Republic country-specific specific configuration. We've always found in Washington an attentive partner and unstinting commitment in terms of helping the CAR. I know you show that devotion to almost all PBC beneficiaries, so thank you again. Now I turn to Mr. Gooden from civil society to ask Often partnerships with civil society remain limited to specific projects, quick impact projects, or civil society organizations play simply advisory role. What tangible changes are necessary to move towards more strategic long-term partnerships, partnerships likely to bolster local capacity and sustain peace?

Thank you very much, Chair. A quick answer is that we need to move from short-term projects to long-term partnerships. I see the Swedish Ambassador sitting here. The Swedish Peace Research Institute did a study that showed that the life cycle of political conflicts is about 20 years. So we're dealing today with very, very complex conflicts. We were— I see the Ambassador of Somalia. We were in Somalia in 1997. We're still supporting peace in Somalia. We've been in the DRC from 1999, Burundi from 1995. So this proves that these are long-term initiatives. Now, I want to make 4 suggestions in that regard. The first is that we must have multi-year flexible financing. The second is that we need joint analysis and joint strategy. In 2 weeks' time, we'll be working with some of our partners on Sudan and South Sudan—joint analysis, again, joint strategy. Thirdly, we need investment in local institutional capacity. Without institutional— Madam, you talked about that. We need to build institutions to sustain peace in countries. Fourthly, we need the Peacebuilding Commission to help create more structured partnerships between governments, civil societies, the UN, the IFIs, and regional organizations. The PBC is uniquely placed to convene these actors around nationally-led prevention strategies. Countries. And lastly, to conclude, Chair, let me say that after 20 years, the next phase of the peacebuilding architecture must be judged not only by how well it will manage crisis, but effectively how well it can prevent crisis. That's going to be the major challenge for the Peacebuilding Commission. Thank you, Chair.

That's our objective for the coming years, I can assure you. I would like to thank Mr. Gordon for for his answers, especially for the action of the accord in the field.

I don't know why I suddenly started speaking English and stopped speaking French, but there you go. My next question is for Mr. Shamsou from UNIPEACE builders. Many organizations led by young people struggle to access flexible and sustained financing in spite of the proven impact those organizations have. In your view, what is the most powerful measure that donors, governments, and international partners could take in order to allow initiatives spearheaded by young people to develop and endure over time?

Thank you very much. This is a very timely question. First one, we need to continue to build trust, trust here in terms of how— what is the essence of what we are doing, because as young people, we are really looking for change, and we are taking initiatives on our own, even without funding, in very difficult circumstances. We are still trying to bring communities together and to build peace, so we need to build that trust. Number 2 is the language. Peacebuilders, young peacebuilders in particular, speak a different language, and the development partners speak a different language. On the other side, development partners are talking about compliance, they're talking about organizational profiles, they're talking about M&E, etc. Young peacebuilders, on the other hand, are looking at how do we improve relations between our friends who are either different religions, different ethnic groups, different political parties, how do we engender this kind of conversation? So we need to bridge that gap that exists. Compliance is important. It's still important to have the young people in the room. So what language can we speak that is universal in a way that young people understand, in a way that donor partners will understand? And again, I'm going to reference the first point I made. That information is already available. For example, in UNOWAI, we have a small funding mechanism that we are able to give small grants to youth-led organizations, and we have produced a report that shares best lessons for donors. So the information is already there. Donors just need to get this information and start applying that. And to conclude, I think one of the things that donors should also do to be able to work with young people is that co-ownership part of it. When you are going to fund the work of youth-led organizations, you need to move beyond just the amount of money you are investing in the organization. You are investing whatever currency it is, they are investing their lives. Look at that and take notice of this investment of their lives, their time, their energies, their leadership into the project, and count that as a contribution to the project. Thank you.
I wish to thank Mr. Shamsu for that response and particularly for his enthusiasm.
Thank you.

My last question for the last speaker, Ms. Dompa from the Adeba Laboratory: What incentives or precise partnerships with governments, the UN, or financing institutions would allow your business to scale up and to become an even more powerful driver of local inclusion and economic resilience?

For me, the key element is skin in the game. There are some amazing initiatives going on on the ground, and we need to make sure that the best ones get the attention. And by best, I define the initiatives that are carried by people who shoulder the consequences when they fail, and that impact the most people when they succeed. So for us, number one, patient capital. Fund the funds like Barkha Capital, or even the RMBN Alliance, who understand that we need to act fast, fast, and could fund companies like mine that have trouble raising money. 2, connect us to markets. Markets scale faster than aid. And if we can have more initiatives in terms of social procurement, or even I was walking to the UN gift shops and I was like, oh, we could have Adéba products here. That could be helpful. That could help us scale faster. And then lastly, I mentioned the ecosystem. We have the UNESCO chair that I mentioned. But Adeba took part in a program that was financed by the World Bank that sent us to Paris so that we could connect with the best industry leaders and then basically give us so much clarity that we accelerated our growth, I think, 5 years. So to summarize, skin in the game.

Je remercie Madame— Hi.

Thank Madame Demba for her response. And we have thus arrived at the conclusion of our panel discussion. I wish to thank all of our distinguished panelists for their enriching contributions and the perspectives that they have shared with us. And I must recognize that what they have shared with us is new ideas and sources of inspiration. The best— is the best way to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the establishment of the BBC, and especially to look towards the future. And by shouldering more accountability, more responsibility, I think that listening to partners on the ground is of critical importance as we seek to ensure that we as diplomats, that we as countries and that we can forge a vision that is more realistic, more pragmatic, and especially to listen to these voices, to listen to their— when it comes to their capabilities and to listen to their perspectives, to reframe our perspectives. Because here in New York, we dream a great deal. We dream of reconciliation. We dream of peace. We dream of what— everything that can improve the world, but you are on the ground and you have more pragmatic, more realistic visions. And in a certain way, this brings us back to the reality, the problems faced by our continents, our countries, especially those areas of conflict and the crises of fragility. Once again, thank you all for your participation. For the opportunity to commemorate together this anniversary and for your contribution with all your— with your ideas and perspectives. Thank you.
Thank you, Tiff.

Excellences, ladies and gentlemen, we will now move to a short segment to commemorate the action of the PBF. It is my pleasure to invite Ambassador Mashale Kamau, Chair of the Advisory— the PBF Advisory Group, to present a short video on the initiatives of the Fund. I would like to state that as we listen to the statement from Mr. Kamau, this is not just a statement from the Advisory Group, but this is also from the architect of the Agenda, the 2030 Agenda, to which he has dedicated a great deal of time and energy and tact as well as statesmanship. So I wish to take this opportunity to thank His Excellency and to commend his diplomacy, multilateralism, and commitment to the United Nations. Jeremy, Ambassador, welcome. Please, you have the floor. Welcome.

Mr. Chairman, thank you very much for that kind introduction. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, the Secretary-General has spoken to the weight of this moment today. Allow me to offer a complementary perspective as someone who has seen peacebuilding from several vantage points. 20 years ago, the Peacebuilding Fund was a simple idea. Now, it stands as one of the most remarkable instruments of this organization. Mr. Chairman, I commend you and you, the members of the PBC, for the support that you have given the Secretary-General's the Peace Building Fund, because without your support, the PBF would not be the organization that it is. Mr. Chairman, as the East African Community's Special Envoy on Eastern DRC, when I was in that role, I came to see how fragile peace can be and how much depends on early action. And as Permanent Representative of Kenya here at the United Nations and Chair of the PBC Commission, I have argued for this Fund in these very halls. And now, as Chair of the Secretary-General's Advisory Group on the Fund, I have examined the evidence of two decades of peacebuilding. The conclusion is a welcome one: peacebuilding and prevention works. And this there is no doubt about. Consider what it means today for the world that this Fund acts without hesitation, that it moves quickly and takes risks that not too many other organizations here at the UN or anywhere else takes. That it entrusts, as we heard from Liberia and Haiti, national leaders and community leaders to build on their own peace plans and stands by them as they do. This brings the United Nations system another partners together, as the Peacebuilding Fund itself does, working hand in hand with the Peacebuilding Commission. Across 20 years, in countries and communities on every continent, this Fund has helped turn fragile moments into longer peace. There is no small investment. It is among the very best of what we can do. And I therefore commend members of states, members of the United Nations who are represented here, who continue to support the Peacebuilding Fund and its Secretariat, both politically and financially. Without your support, the Peacebuilding Fund would simply not be able to do what it does. So we thank you for your support. Let us now take a moment to recognize what you have supported for 20 years. The achievements that we can celebrate today, as well as the challenges that lie ahead, will be seen and understood during this particular video.. And it is my pleasure to introduce the short video on the PBF, and as it is narrated by our Special Assistant Secretary-General Elizabeth Spehar, who is a champion of the PBF and is also a great supporter of us, the Member States, in this work.

I thank you very much, and I welcome you to We all know there's a record level of conflicts raging around the world, and we have more and more complicated conflict scenarios. We have the estimates of 20,000 people a month that will be losing their lives over violent conflict in this year. The problems are multidimensional. Peacebuilding is designed to try to help member states to address that. So really, peacebuilding is about looking at the root causes of conflict. What are the things that are driving conflict in a society? And creating the conditions that will make conflict less likely in a country. The peacebuilding journey will often include rebuilding basic institutions, rebuilding the possibility for livelihoods, reconciliation, transitional justice, in other words, making sure that the victims of human rights violations during conflict will be addressed. For example, the Colombian peace process and peace agreement, a lot of that was predicated on justice for the victims and addressing the past. In a way that would allow Colombian society to heal. The Fund was set up to be able to work through the UN system and utilize a lot of our UN partners, you know, agencies, funds, and programs, to support member states along what we call the peace continuum: before a conflict erupts, during, and after, to build and sustain sustain peace in their societies. So we really are based on national ownership, and the peacebuilding journey of each and every country will be somewhat different. The Peacebuilding Fund has now invested over $2 billion across the world since 2006 when it started operating. These resources have gone to 75 countries through 24 UN entities and that's also involved over 80 civil society organizations. We've done some important work in countries like Colombia, Guatemala, Sierra Leone, Liberia to support the implementation of their peace agreements or dialogue processes. One of the roles that we play in terms of the UN system in places like Central African Republic is to work closely particularly with the peacekeeping operation that's there, to make sure that the peacekeeping gains, for example, of MINUSCA, will not be lost as eventually that mission starts to transition out. The world cannot afford more conflict. We can't afford more deaths, more destruction, and the economic consequences of that. We're all paying for it in so many different ways. Really, the world is ripe for more peacebuilding funding and more use of the Peacebuilding Fund if indeed we ourselves can garner the resources to keep playing our role. It's the smartest investment that we can make.

I thank Ambassador Masharyeff for his statement and especially for the light he has shed on the work of the PBF, which he has been chairing for a number of I wish to convey to him the fact that through his chairmanship of the PBF, he has instilled energy, a visionary approach, and galvanized efforts and introduced a conviction which is— which dovetails with— which is reflected in all of his statements and efforts. I thank the ASDB G. Sbeharr for the high-quality statement, video statement. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we now move to the list of speakers. I invite member states to speak from their seats. I wish to remind delegations that statements are limited to 3 minutes. The microphone light will blink— will begin to blink at 2 minutes 30, and they will automatically be cut off after 3 minutes. I now first give the floor to representatives, to be followed by those speaking on behalf of delegations. Mr. Sebastian Rogaš, Director-General for Multilateral Affairs of Croatia, has the floor.

Mr. Chair, Madam Assistant Secretary General Speicher, Excellencies. We mark 20 years of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture. It is a moment to recognize progress and raise our collective ambition. Over two decades, the Peacebuilding Commission, the Peacebuilding Fund, and the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office have shown that prevention, national ownership, and strong partnerships help countries move from fragility towards lasting peace. Croatia has been engaged from the start, contributing to the PBC's creation, serving most recently as Chair in 2023 and now as Vice Chair. Our own experience confirms that peace, development and humanitarian action must advance together. Two national examples illustrate this. First, mine action was essential for restoring security and enabling development. Once, Croatia had over 1,000 square kilometers contaminated by mines. The last mine was removed this year. In the meantime, we became demining champions. This saved lives and unlocked economic recovery. Second, the search for the still missing 1,725 persons from our homeland war in the 1990s remains our humanitarian priority. We continue to seek still-denied access to archives and, as co-chair of the Global Alliance for the Missing, support international efforts in this area. On both topics, Croatia offers cooperation and help worldwide. These experiences show that sustainable peace requires inclusion, recovery, economic opportunity and justice. The latest review of the peacebuilding architecture, with its focus on prevention, sustaining peace and national prevention strategies, aligns with this understanding. The review also underscores the importance of broad partnerships with regional organizations, international financial institutions, civil society and the private sector. Such cooperation brings the expertise and legitimacy needed to address complex drivers of conflict. The PBC must continue strengthening its cooperation with the General Assembly and the Security Council while deepening its bridging role with ECOSOC. Croatia, as an ECOSOC member, PBC vice-chair, and candidate for the Security Council for the term 2030-31, Croatia remains committed to advancing coherence across all three UN pillars. The Peace Building Fund remains the UN's most agile and catalytic financing tool. Croatia has supported it from the beginning with more than $400,000 and will continue advocating for stronger pooled and blended financing.

So sorry, Mr. Director General.

I thank the Director General for Multilateral Affairs of Croatia, and it is my pleasure to give the floor now to Her Excellency Madame Katarina Arendt, Director General for European Union Affairs of Germany.

Mr. Chairman, Excellencies, dear colleagues. Germany aligns itself with the statement of the European Union. It is a pleasure to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the inception of the Peace Building Fund, as well as the anniversary of the inaugural meeting of the Peace Building Commission in June 2006. In these 20 years, the Peace Building Commission has accompanied over 30 countries and regions on their national peace building journeys. The Peace Building Fund has supported innovative initiatives initiatives in over 70 contexts. As biggest donor to the PBF, former chair and current vice chair of the PBC, the lesson we have learned throughout this journey is the following: peacebuilding is a continuous endeavor that is only possible through close partnerships. Guatemala, Liberia, and Haiti, as we have heard, are excellent examples 3 countries in different stages of conflict and reconciliation that show what can be achieved when all relevant actors team up in support of a nationally-led process. The peacebuilding architecture is the enabler for these Partnerships for Peace. As member states, we have created this system that enables us to support each other in building and sustaining peace together. Yet the UN system itself faces significant challenges at the moment. While the number of conflicts rises, the UN system is increasingly under strain and the available funding for peace and security is shrinking. Now more than ever, we need a peacebuilding architecture that is adequately financed to provide fast and flexible support for national peacebuilding and prevention efforts when needed. And we need a Secretariat that is adequately resourced to support the PBC, to manage the PBF, and to bring the hinge function of the peacebuilding architecture to life by connecting its core bodies to the broader peacebuilding landscape, both within and outside of the UN. Having successfully adopted last year's peacebuilding architecture review, Now it is time to seize the opportunity to create a broader and inclusive peacebuilding architecture. An architecture that complements the aims of the UN80 Initiative by increasing effectiveness through meaningful partnerships.

Thank you. I thank the Director-General for European Union Affairs of Germany. And I give the floor now to Her Excellency Madame Gillian Rae, Director of Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division of Australia.

Thank you, Chair. This year marks two decades of the UN peacebuilding architecture, 20 years of advancing peace and stability, strengthening partnerships, and championing conflict prevention. Australia has been proud to be part of this from the outset. In 2015, alongside Angola, Australia co-facilitated the Peacebuilding Architecture Review that gave rise to the Sustaining Peace Agenda. Today, we are a member of the Peacebuilding Commission and a leading donor to the Peacebuilding Fund. But with conflicts growing in frequency and complexity, we must do more. I will make 3 points. We must invest in evidence-based prevention. This week, Australia launched new policy guidance for national prevention strategies, a practical voluntary resource to support member states and partners invest earlier. Because peacebuilding finance remains profoundly underfunded, dwarfed by global military spending and falling drastically short of what is needed, our policy guidance is about closing this financing gap, to make the case for nationally-led prevention, an investment which we know has extraordinary returns. Second, we must strengthen the UN's architecture. We must shift from reacting to crises to preventing them. We must address root causes such as poverty, exclusion, inequality, and climate change. We must advance the inclusion of women, Youth and Indigenous peoples. And we must be clear, protecting people is central to building and sustaining peace. As a candidate for the UN Security Council for 2029 and 2030, Australia will focus on both preventing conflict and protecting those affected by it. We will drive practical initiatives that promote peace, uphold the rules-based order, and strengthen accountability. This is why we worked with partners to launch the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, which renews commitment to protecting those delivering life-saving assistance in conflict zones. And finally, we must maintain focus on the Indo-Pacific, a region which has growing conflict risks as well as world-leading responses. We will amplify approaches such as the the Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration, and the ASEAN-Australia Joint Leaders' Statement on Conflict Prevention and Crisis Management. These are powerful statements of regional resolve that make clear our shared desire for peace and stability. Chair, after 20 years, there is much to be proud of, but still much more to do. We must invest in prevention if we want peace, and we must act early. Through renewed commitment and collective action, we can move towards lasting peace for the next 20 years and beyond. I thank you.

I thank the Director of Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division of Australia, and I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Lukasz Żelenski, Deputy Director of the Department of Global Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Poland.

Thank you very much, Excellency. As a country that has worked hard to rebuild its security institutions and resilience after democratic transformation of 1989, Poland understands that sustainable peace takes long-term commitment, strong institutions, and real investment. Peacebuilding is not just about stopping conflict, it's about building the conditions for stability security, development, and opportunity. With that experience in mind, we want to share our perspective as we mark the 20th anniversary of the Peacebuilding Commission. Over the past two decades, the Commission has grown into a truly unique platform within the UN system—one that brings together political, development, humanitarian, and financial actors in support of sustaining peace. This anniversary carries special meaning for Poland. As a member of the Commission during its 18th and 19th sessions, as well as Vice Chair of the Bureau, we saw firsthand how the Commission bridges diverse stakeholders and promotes integrated approaches to peacebuilding. That experience has only strengthened our belief in its value. We therefore welcome the stronger role envisioned for the Commission in the 2025 Twin Resolutions. Poland particularly values the Commission's support for for nationally owned prevention and building strategies. The most successful peacebuilding efforts are those driven by national priorities and backed by inclusive institutions that can address the root causes of instability. We also welcome the stronger focus on impact and follow-up. The Commission's relevance will increasingly depend on its ability to turn dialogue into concrete results and track measurable progress on the on the ground. I will make 3 points. First, address the root causes of conflict. While focusing on the most imperative needs of the countries concerned, peacebuilding should also take a long-term view, directing resources to key areas such as poverty eradication, education, job creation, and livelihood improvement, strengthening countries' endogenous development capacity, and addressing the deep-rooted causes of conflict and instability. Second, keep the work on the right track. Peacebuilding must respect the sovereignty and ownership of the countries concerned, adopt targeted measures based on their specific conditions and priorities, and genuinely respect, mobilize, and give full play to their leading role. The nexus between peacebuilding and peacekeeping should be strengthened to promote a balanced transition from peacekeeping to peacebuilding. Third, pool resources and capacity. In line with this mandate, the PPC should strengthen interaction with the GA, the Security Council, and ECOSOC, enhance coordination with UN system programs and funds, actively expand partnerships with regional organizations and IFIs, mobilize resources effectively, strengthen system-wide synergy, and continuously improve quality and efficiency Chair, China has put forward the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, and the Global Civilization Initiative, and the Global Governance Initiative, contributing Chinese wisdom and solutions to international peacebuilding. We are ready to deepen exchange of experience with all parties, actively participate in implementing the review outcomes, promote a more practical, efficient, and inclusive peacebuilding architecture and work together for a future of peace and prosperity. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of China, and I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Colombia.

Gracias. Thank you, Chair. Colombia's history has proven that peace is much more than the absence of armed conflict. Lasting peace requires justice, inclusion, and dignity. It requires transforming the root causes of violence: inequality, poverty, the lack of access to land, the absence of opportunities, environmental degradation, and the historic divides that have caused our society to crack. Those problems must be resolved. As such, we insist that peace, sustainable development, and the effective guarantee of human rights are inextricably linked. In Colombia, our efforts to build peace have been first and foremost an exercise in social and territorial-level transformation. Social cohesion, inclusive governance, and human rights are essential pillars to prevent conflicts and sustain peace over time. We have learned that diversity is our greatest asset and that words are more powerful than weapons. On our journey, the Peacebuilding Commission and Peacebuilding Fund, as well as the Security Council and international partners that have chosen to put their full weight behind peace in Colombia, have been crucial allies. Colombia's experience means that we can now reaffirm the value of South-South and triangular cooperation as a tool to build peace. Through our initiative, From Colombia to the World, we have helped other countries to make use of our experience by sharing lessons in transitional justice, reincorporation, and reparation to victims. We also reaffirm the central role that the Women, Peace and Security and Youth, Peace and Security agendas play. Peace requires the voices, leadership, and effective participation of those who historically have sustained life and hope in the midst of violence. Colombia will continue, Chair, to provide the Commission with its experience, this born of the conviction that peace is a collective cause, one which demands persistence, solidarity, and sustained political commitment. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Colombia, and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Kenya.

Thank you, Chair. Kenya thanks the Peace Building Commission for convening this meeting. We acknowledge the PPC's value as a unique advisory, bridging, and convening platform, fostering greater coherence, partnership, and sustaining international support for countries peacebuilding priorities, especially those emerging from conflict and at risk of instability. We also acknowledge the catalytic role of the PPF in helping countries strengthen national prevention capacities, enhance women and youth engagement, promote social cohesion, and respond to emerging risks. The growing collaboration between the PPC and the international financial institutions —reflect a deeper recognition that peace and development are mutually reinforcing and that investment in governance, livelihoods, and resilience are essential to sustaining peace. In this regard, we reaffirm our support for further strengthening its effectiveness, inclusivity, and impact, which should begin with implementation of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review Resolution. As a PPC member, Kenya has learned several lessons over the last decade. First, peacebuilding is most effective when national ownership is matched with international solidarity and the prevention is supported by enduring political, technical, and financial commitment. Second, peacebuilding cannot be achieved by any one actor alone. Rather, Sustainable outcomes depend on coordinated efforts among national and local actors, working in concert with the United Nations system, regional organizations, and IFIs. Third, by acting on early warning signs, strengthening institutions, and building resilience, risks can be addressed before they escalate into crisis, helping to reduce the human political and economic costs of conflict and instability. Kenya's National Peacebuilding Act is a testament of the value of such an integrated approach. Through our whole-of-government and whole-of-society framework, national institutions work alongside communities, civil society, and local leaders to advance conflict prevention and social cohesion. Going forward, Kenya calls for the integrated support for the work of the PPC, including through sustained funding, enhanced partnership, and system-wide collaborations. I thank you.
I thank the permanent Deputy Permanent Representative of Kenya, and I now give the floor to the Ambassador of the United Kingdom to ECOSOC.

Thank you, Chair. Excellencies, the United Kingdom is pleased and proud to mark 20 years of the UN peacebuilding architecture. This milestone comes at an important moment as we come here together in this first Peacebuilding Week and following the successful 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review. The UK reaffirms today our longstanding commitment to preventing conflict and building sustainable peace. Over the past two decades, the UN peacebuilding architecture has proven its value, strengthening international coordination, supporting countries through critical transitions, and helping to address the root causes of conflict. The Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund in particular has played a unique role, delivering timely catalytic support in fragile contexts and enabling the UN system them to respond more coherently and effectively. With the highest level of armed conflict globally since World War II, increasing pressure on financial resources, our collective efforts to prevent conflict and sustain peace are more essential now than ever. The 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review reflected strong member state consensus to build on what works whilst going further. Strengthening UN system-wide coherence to ensure greater impact at country level, deepening support for nationally owned prevention, and working more closely with partners, including international financial institutions, civil society, as well as, of course, local communities. The PBF is central to delivering these ambitions. As we look ahead to the strategy refresh, there is clear opportunity to sharpen comparative advantage— and focus in a more resource-constrained environment. The Fund should concentrate its resources where they can make the greatest difference, targeting the most critical conflict risks, guided by robust early warning and political analysis. The PBF is most effective when it becomes fast, flexible, and catalytic, and is behind nationally-led prevention and peacebuilding efforts., including involving those closest to conflict, particularly women. In this context, the UK continues to back the Fund. Since 2006, the United Kingdom has contributed over £200 million in UN peacebuilding efforts, and we will provide a further £3.2 million this year, demonstrating our commitment. The Peacebuilding Architecture Review has given us a strong foundation Our shared task now is implementation. Thank you.
I thank the Ambassador of the United Kingdom to ECOSOC, and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Rwanda.

Thank you very much, Chair, for giving us the floor. We join others in marking 20 years of our peacebuilding architecture. Peacebuilding architecture turns 20 when time of conflicts are increasing, humanitarian needs are growing, development sources are becoming more constrained, and therefore it's important to reflect on what worked and where we need to do better. Mr. Chair and colleagues, the theme you provided for this meeting, Three Ideas are great for reflection: partnerships, innovations, and impact. The first lesson from last years of peacebuilding is that partnership matters. Peacebuilding works best when governments, regional organizations, international institutions, and everyone works together. No single actor can build peace alone. The second lesson is that prevention remains one of the smartest investments we can ever make, yet we continue to spend far more responding to crisis than preventing them. If we want different outcomes, we must make a different choice. Finally, impact is what most— which is what matters most. 20 years on, successful— the success of this architecture must be measured whether people feel better, whether institutions are more resilient, and whether communities have better confidence in their future. As we implement the outcome of 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review, Rwanda would welcome a stronger focus on prevention, more predictable financing, and a closer look at partnerships across the UN system. The next chapter of peacebuilding must be judged by one thing: whether it makes a meaningful difference in people's lives. And I thank you.

Je vous remercie.
