Ntshimkhize: Chair, Excellencies, colleagues. This commemoration provides a timely opportunity to reflect on how partnerships across national actors, the UN system, civil society, international financial institutions, and the Peacebuilding Fund have strengthened peacebuilding efforts and supported countries in navigating emerging challenges. South Africa considers peacebuilding as one of the most cost-effective investments the international community can make in consolidating peace efforts and enabling a sustainable path to development. Effective peacebuilding prevents the emergence and re-emergence of conflict by addressing its root causes, reduces humanitarian need, strengthens institutions, and creates the foundations for sustainable development. The opportunity cost of not investing is far greater. However, when support is inconsistent or under-resourced, countries face heightened risks of relapse, prolonged crises, displacement, and the erosion of hard-won, won gains. If we fail to sustain support, we will pay significantly more in financial, social,— and human terms to respond to crises that could have been prevented. South Africa calls for a decisive shift towards coherent, predictable and adequately financed UN peacebuilding support at the country level and in line with national priorities. Given the complex and interconnected nature of peacebuilding efforts across the three pillars of the UN, The UN system must break down silos and deliver integrated, context-specific assistance anchored in national ownership. Chairperson, ahead of the 2030 Review, South Africa commits to continue our positive engagement within the Peacebuilding Commission to advance impactful and coherent peacebuilding. We will champion stronger partnerships and coherence with regional efforts such as the African Union-led Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development Initiatives. We will also continue to advocate for increased and predictable financing for the Peacebuilding Fund, as well as for a more meaningful role for women and youth in peacebuilding efforts, and promote knowledge sharing on inclusive, nationally-driven peacebuilding approaches. Perspectives, but particularly from African contexts. I thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of South Africa for the statement. I now give the floor to the Permanent Observer of CARICOM.

Mr. Chair, Excellencies, as we commemorate the 20th anniversary of the PBC and the PBF, We celebrate two decades of partnership, prevention, and peacebuilding that have helped countries navigate crises, strengthen institutions, and lay the foundations for lasting peace. Allow me to share the experience of CARICOM's partnership with Haiti, which demonstrates the important contribution that regional organizations can make to peacebuilding through dialogue, good offices, and sustained political accompaniment. Through its eminent persons group created by the heads of state and government of CARICOM, our regional organization has worked alongside Haiti, its international partners, and Haitian stakeholders to reach agreements to establish transitional presidential council in 2024, and the follow-on transitional arrangement in 2026. This experience demonstrates the value of regional diplomacy, good offices, and inclusive dialogue in consolidating political gains and building consensus around lasting solutions. At the same time, political gains must be matched by humanitarian institutional and development support, as well as security, if they are to endure. This is why CARICOM supports the Gang Suppression Force as Haiti moves towards a more robust response to armed gangs and the restoration of security and state authority. Mr. Chair, looking ahead, the most important change we would like to see from the 2025 PBAR is stronger, more predictable, and better coordinated support for nationally led peacebuilding priorities backed by sustainable financing. In that regard, we welcome the engagement of the PBF in Haiti and the ring-fencing of resources from the UN regular budget to support peacebuilding activities. Even modest investments rooted in local needs can have a catalytic impact. As others have said, Mr. Chair, peacebuilding is smart investment. I thank you, Mr.

Thank you, Mr. President, and Thank you for organizing today's annual session. Against this backdrop,, we need to reflect on their increasing role in the times we are living. PBC remains the UN's unique intergovernmental platform, sustaining attention when peace is most fragile and convening a variety of actors around nationally owned priorities. I want to make 3 points. As we all know these days, consensus is more an exception than expected result. Second, the national ownership remains the foundation of sustainable peace. Peacebuilding therefore needs to be anchored in genuine partnerships with all relevant stakeholders. Youth must be recognized not only as beneficiaries, but as partners and leaders in shaping peaceful and resilient societies. The UN Peacebuilding Week can help fast-forwarding PBC relevance as an annual platform for inclusive dialogue and greater visibility of peacebuilding. It can serve as a checklist for our responsibility. I thank you.

Distinguished Chair, Excellencies, and fellow participants, I thank you, Chair, for convening this milestone event, and we take note with interest the important, timely messages shared by the Secretary-General and other distinguished speakers. As we commemorate this important milestone, of the 20th anniversary of the UN Peacebuilding Architecture, and very aptly during this Peacebuilding Week, Papua New Guinea recognizes and pays special tribute to the UN Peacebuilding Architecture for being an important cornerstone supporting the United Nations Charter principle mandate on peace and security and the well-being and dignity of humanity, especially at a time the world is challenged by the current geopolitical landscape and its associated issues. Papua New Guinea recognizes the evolving and adaptive manner in which the peacebuilding architecture has made a mark around the world and at the institutional level, as shown by the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund, which Papua New Guinea has increasingly benefited from and for which we are grateful for. This is an important opportunity not only for us to reflect on the progress we have made and the challenges that require us to address, but also to renew our collective political commitment, leadership, and faith to conflict prevention and peacebuilding and sustaining peace through nationally-led, owned, and driven solutions, and complemented by sustained partnerships in a meaningful and practical way. Anchored by the peacebuilding architecture. One of the most fundamental lessons for us, which is in part inspired by the peacebuilding architecture is the critical importance of peace through peaceful means. Through the welcome support of the PBF since 2016 and PBC and other multilateral and bilateral development partners, it has ably assisted us in our ongoing Bougainville peace process, where there has been unbroken peace for 25 years now, and most recently in another part of our country, the level of support given—

Chair, at the outset, we wish to thank Morocco, current chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, for convening this annual session. We welcome the holding of the first Peacebuilding Week in the United Nations. It was one of the commitments reached in resolutions adopted in 2025 in order to strengthen the peacebuilding Architecture at the United Nations. Chair Spain, since it's in— since the PBC's inception has supported it in these years, it has proven its added value in contributing to stability and post-conflict recovery. It's vital to strengthen the role it plays in the UN system, particularly in connection with the General Assembly, the Security Council, and ECOSOC. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Pakistan congratulates you on convening this important annual session as we mark 20 years of the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peace Building Fund. This milestone provides an opportunity not only to reflect on the lessons learned, but to renew our collective commitment to peace building in an increasingly fragile and polarized world. Pakistan firmly believes in the peace continuum approach, one that recognizes that prevention, peacemaking, peacekeeping, peace building, and development are not isolated but interconnected parts of a holistic effort to Sustainable peace and development. Experience has shown that ending violence alone does not secure peace. Peace can best be sustained when societies begin to experience its dividends, when institutions regain legitimacy, trust is restored, opportunities expand, and people see tangible improvements in their daily lives. Sustainable peace requires strong institutions, social cohesion, economic opportunities, and nationally-owned pathways to recovery. Sustainable peace cannot be imposed. It must be built, owned, and led by national actors with the full support of an engaged international community. In this regard, Pakistan shares the concern about the growing challenges to multilateral commitments that underpin peacebuilding, including on financing and normative frameworks. Pakistan strongly supports the work of the Peacebuilding Fund as an important instrument for translating political commitments into practical impact on the ground. Its flexibility, catalytic nature, and responsiveness to national priorities make it indispensable within the broader peacebuilding architecture. It is encouraging to hear today, including from the countries who have benefited from PBC and PBF, on how partnerships supported by the Fund have delivered meaningful results for communities. Moving ahead, Partnerships must be prioritized and remain firmly aligned with national priorities. The New Peacebuilding Architecture was itself an innovation designed to harness inclusion and enhance impact. At 20, the Peacebuilding Architecture should inspire renewed confidence that multilateral cooperation can still deliver sustainable peace. I thank you, Mr. Chairman.
